title: Meiosis: passing genetic information between generations

curriculum.source_reference: Cambridge International AS & A Level Biology 9700 (2025–2027), Topic 16.1, syllabus pp. 40–41, learning outcomes 1–7. https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664560-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf

learning_objectives: Explain homologous chromosome pairs and distinguish homologous chromosomes from sister chromatids.
Explain why meiosis is a reduction division in gamete production.
Describe chromosome, nuclear-envelope, cell-surface-membrane and spindle behaviour through the eight named stages of meiosis.
Identify meiotic stages from diagrams and photomicrographs.
Explain how crossing over and independent assortment produce genetically different gametes.
Explain how random fertilisation increases genetic variation among offspring.

sections.heading: Ploidy: haploid and diploid
sections.body: A diploid nucleus (2n) contains two sets of chromosomes. In a typical diploid animal cell, one chromosome of each homologous pair was inherited from each parent. A haploid nucleus (n) contains one set of chromosomes. Human body cells are diploid with 46 chromosomes; human gametes are haploid with 23. The symbols n and 2n describe sets of chromosomes, not the amount of DNA present at a particular moment. After DNA replication, a cell remains diploid even though each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids.

sections.heading: Homologous chromosomes and sister chromatids
sections.body: Homologous chromosomes are a pair, one maternal and one paternal, that carry the same genes at corresponding loci. They may carry different alleles. They are similar in length, centromere position and gene loci. Sister chromatids are the two copies of one chromosome produced by DNA replication; they are joined at the centromere until they separate. Do not call homologous chromosomes sister chromatids.

sections.heading: Why meiosis is necessary
sections.body: Meiosis produces haploid gametes from diploid cells. At fertilisation, two haploid nuclei fuse and restore the diploid chromosome number. If gametes were diploid, fertilisation would double the chromosome number in each generation. Meiosis therefore maintains a stable chromosome number across generations in a species with a diploid-dominant life cycle.

sections.heading: Before meiosis: DNA replication
sections.body: DNA replicates once during interphase before meiosis begins. Each chromosome then consists of two genetically identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere. There is no second DNA replication between meiosis I and meiosis II. The two divisions distribute the replicated chromosomes into four haploid products.

sections.heading: Meiosis I: separating homologous chromosomes
sections.body: Prophase I: chromosomes condense; homologous chromosomes pair; crossing over may occur between non-sister chromatids; the nuclear envelope breaks down and spindle microtubules form. Metaphase I: homologous pairs align at the equator in random orientations and attach to spindle fibres. Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles; centromeres do not divide and sister chromatids remain joined. Telophase I: chromosomes reach the poles; nuclei may reform and cytokinesis divides the cell. The result is two haploid cells, although each chromosome still consists of two chromatids. Meiosis I is the reduction division.

sections.heading: Meiosis II: separating sister chromatids
sections.body: There is no DNA replication between the two divisions. Prophase II: chromosomes condense again if necessary, nuclear envelopes break down and new spindles form. Metaphase II: chromosomes align singly at the equator. Anaphase II: centromeres divide and sister chromatids separate to opposite poles. Telophase II: nuclear envelopes reform and cytokinesis produces four haploid cells. The products are genetically different because crossing over and independent assortment have generated different combinations of alleles.

sections.heading: Crossing over
sections.body: During prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair closely. Non-sister chromatids can break and rejoin at corresponding positions, exchanging equivalent DNA segments. This produces recombinant chromatids with new combinations of alleles. Crossing over does not normally exchange whole chromosomes, and it is not the separation of sister chromatids. It increases variation among gametes.

sections.heading: Independent assortment
sections.body: At metaphase I, each homologous pair can orient in either direction independently of the other pairs. The maternal or paternal homolog that moves to a pole for one chromosome pair does not determine which homolog moves to that pole for another pair. This creates different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes in gametes. For a cell with n chromosome pairs, independent assortment alone can produce 2^n possible chromosome combinations, before considering crossing over.

sections.heading: Random fertilisation
sections.body: Any one genetically different haploid gamete may fuse with any compatible gamete from the other parent. Random fusion combines two independently generated sets of alleles, creating a genetically unique zygote. Variation therefore arises through crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation.

sections.heading: Recognising stages in diagrams and photomicrographs
sections.body: Look for paired homologous chromosomes at the equator in metaphase I; homologous chromosomes moving apart while sister chromatids remain joined in anaphase I; individual chromosomes aligned at the equator in metaphase II; and sister chromatids moving apart in anaphase II. Count centromeres and chromosome units carefully. A replicated chromosome is still counted as one chromosome until its centromere divides and sister chromatids separate. In photomicrographs, use chromosome arrangement and movement rather than relying only on the apparent number of cells.

sections.heading: Meiosis compared with mitosis
sections.body: Both processes follow DNA replication and use spindle fibres to move chromosomes. Mitosis has one nuclear division and normally produces two genetically similar daughter nuclei with the same chromosome-set number as the parent. Meiosis has two nuclear divisions, pairs homologous chromosomes in prophase I, separates homologous chromosomes in meiosis I and sister chromatids in meiosis II, and produces four haploid products that are genetically different. Meiosis includes crossing over and independent assortment; these are not normal features of mitosis.

sections.heading: Exam technique: describe chromosome behaviour precisely
sections.body: Use the correct pair of structures for each division. In anaphase I, homologous chromosomes separate. In anaphase II, sister chromatids separate after centromeres divide. State that the spindle attaches to chromosomes and moves them towards opposite poles. Include nuclear-envelope breakdown and reformation where relevant. Do not say that DNA replicates twice or that meiosis I directly produces four gametes.

worked_examples.prompt: A diploid cell has 2n = 8. State the chromosome number in each gamete after meiosis and explain the change.
steps: The diploid cell has four homologous pairs, so 2n = 8.
Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, reducing the number of sets from two to one.
Meiosis II separates sister chromatids without changing the number of chromosome sets.
worked_examples.answer: Each gamete is haploid and has n = 4 chromosomes.
worked_examples.common_error: Do not say n = 8. Haploid means half the diploid chromosome number.

worked_examples.prompt: Explain why a chromosome remains one chromosome after DNA replication even though it contains two chromatids.
steps: DNA replication produces two sister chromatids.
The chromatids remain joined at one centromere.
They are counted as separate chromosomes only when the centromere divides and they separate.
worked_examples.answer: It is one replicated chromosome made of two sister chromatids until separation.
worked_examples.common_error: Do not count each chromatid as a separate chromosome before centromere division.

worked_examples.prompt: Explain how meiosis and fertilisation maintain chromosome number while generating variation.
steps: Meiosis halves the chromosome-set number to form haploid gametes.
Fertilisation fuses two haploid nuclei and restores diploidy.
Crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation produce different allele combinations.
worked_examples.answer: Reduction division prevents chromosome doubling; random and recombined gametes create variation.
worked_examples.common_error: Do not claim fertilisation itself halves the chromosome number.

practice.question: Distinguish homologous chromosomes from sister chromatids.
practice.answer: Homologous chromosomes are maternal and paternal versions with the same genes at corresponding loci and may have different alleles. Sister chromatids are replicated copies of one chromosome joined at a centromere.
mark_points: One from each parent for homologues

practice.question: Describe the events of anaphase I and anaphase II.
practice.answer: In anaphase I, homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles while centromeres do not divide and sister chromatids remain joined. In anaphase II, centromeres divide and sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
mark_points: Centromeres remain intact in anaphase I
Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II

practice.question: Explain two ways meiosis generates genetically different gametes.
practice.answer: Crossing over exchanges corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes in prophase I. Independent assortment results from random orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I, producing different maternal and paternal chromosome combinations.

practice.question: A species has 2n = 14. How many chromosomes are present in a cell at metaphase II?
practice.answer: 7 chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids.
mark_points: Each chromosome remains replicated at metaphase II

practice.question: Why is random fertilisation an additional source of genetic variation?
practice.answer: Any genetically different haploid gamete can fuse with any compatible gamete from the other parent, creating a new combination of alleles in the zygote.

common_mistakes: Confusing homologous chromosomes with sister chromatids.
Saying that centromeres divide in anaphase I.
Saying that DNA replicates before meiosis II.
Calling meiosis I equational rather than reduction division.
Claiming crossing over occurs between sister chromatids.
Describing independent assortment as random separation of sister chromatids in meiosis I.
Counting chromatids as separate chromosomes before centromere division.

questions: When does crossing over occur and between which chromatids?
How does independent assortment create variation?
answers: Prophase I, between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
Homologous pairs orient randomly at metaphase I, giving different maternal/paternal combinations.
Two haploid nuclei fuse, restoring two chromosome sets.
